messages:
sam: Heads-up — during the latest soak we saw what looks like dupe responses for the same prefix after a demote+handback. Not 100% sure if it's stale-read or a double-apply.

kevin: Ugh. Can you paste the minimal repro logs?

sam: Sure, here's the snippet (trimmed):
```
[2026-03-22T18:12:10Z] demote: prefix=tenant42/foo epoch=987 handback_token=tok:55
[2026-03-22T18:12:10Z] apply: write(key=tenant42/foo:bar, v=1) -> ok
[2026-03-22T18:12:11Z] handback: accepted token=tok:55
[2026-03-22T18:12:11Z] read: key=tenant42/foo:bar -> v=0 (stale)
```

tina: Stale after handback... could be race where KV reader hits the old owner before new owner has warmup applied. Did the handback path wait for local prefill/resume?

sam: It did a fast handback path (no prefill) — we tried to optimize latency.

lia: Important question: are we guaranteeing read-after-write (R/W) for handback owner during the window? Our contracts are a bit vague here. I thought handback was supposed to be single-writer strong for the prefix once token accepted.

kevin: Contract we documented: "after handback accepted, new owner must observe all prior successful writes for that prefix". But that assumes writes flowed through the sequencer and persisted. If a write applied to the old owner but hadn't fully propagated to the shared store or tombstone index, new owner might miss it.

sam: Right. In this case the write goes to old owner, handback then completes, and a read shortly after hit a cache warm path on the new owner that hadn't fetched the latest apply.

tina: Do we have a unique incrementing generation/epoch attached to writes that the new owner can use to detect gaps?

kevin: We do: epoch + op_seq. But we're not currently checking on handback acceptance that the new owner has caught up to the op_seq for that prefix. We just trust the token semantics.

lia: Sounds like two remediation options: (1) make handback synchronous and block until prefill/catchup to op_seq, or (2) allow fast handback but mark prefix as "warm-warm" (degraded) and forward reads to old owner/ sequencer until prefill completes. Tradeoffs: (1) adds latency on handback during churn; (2) adds complexity in read-path forwarding and routing.

sam: For production, blocking handback could increase tail latency during eviction storms. We saw that before and it spiked 95p.

kevin: Could we do a hybrid: handback accepts, new owner returns a hint header for clients: X-Prefix-Ready: false, and the internal read path checks that flag and falls back to sequencer for the small window? That keeps external handback latency low but preserves correctness for reads.

tina: The hitch is how clients interact — our API doesn't currently surface that header at the Redwood layer (we'd leak implementation detail). But internal SDK calls could use it.

lia: Another idea: piggyback the last-applied op_seq onto the handback token validation. When old owner signs the handback token it includes last_applied_seq=N; new owner refuses to serve reads until it has observed >=N. Signing ensures we don't get mismatched claims.

kevin: That requires the old owner to be sure N represents durable apply. If N is only in-memory, problem persists. So the old owner must persist a checkpoint or ensure replication.

sam: In our env the old owner flushes a light write-through to the shared index on every apply? Not always — small writes might be in the local write buffer until compaction.

tina: Hmm. Option: on demote, force a tiny durable commit for the prefix (op_seq checkpoint) before emitting token. Cheap but adds IO per demote. Frequency? Eviction storms could make it expensive.

lia: How frequent are demotes in normal operation? In our sim we saw bursts during scale-down and during tenant hotkey shifts. Not constant. I think occasional extra IO might be acceptable for correctness if we can batch commits for multiple prefixes.

kevin: We should quantify cost: add a metric for demote-sync-latency and IO rate in a canary. If spike is within tolerable bounds, go with checkpoint-on-demote + token-with-seq. Otherwise fallback to read-forwarding for the short warm window.

sam: Agreed. Implementation plan suggestion:
- Add handback token payload {epoch, last_durable_seq} signed by old owner
- New owner marks prefix state = warming until local seq >= last_durable_seq
- While warming, new owner's read path forwards to sequencer/old owner for that prefix (fast path)
- Emit telemetry + gate via feature flag

tina: Forwarding per-read could affect latency for hot tenants but it's only for short windows. We should also add a short TTL cache so that we don't forward repeatedly.

lia: Also add a safety net: if warming doesn't finish after X seconds, trigger an async reconcile job that forces a full prefill and alert.

kevin: One more thought: instead of read-forward, could the new owner perform an optimistic prefetch of changed keys on first read and block only the first read? That keeps subsequent reads local. But that first-read block might be surprising for some SLOs.

sam: I like the token-with-seq + warming + forwarding combo. Minimizes tail while preserving correctness. We can run it behind a flag and stress it.

lia: OK. Can someone put up an RFC PR with the token schema, read-path fork, and telemetry plan? Call out costs for demote-checkpoint as alternative.

kevin: I'll draft the RFC. Will include a quick perf microbenchmark and a canary rollout checklist.

ops-bot: Note added: created issue #RM-1214 for RFC + canary. Assigned kevin. :white_check_mark:

sam: Thanks — tagging @oncall for visibility in case we need rollback knobs during canary. :pray:

tina: Thanks all. Appreciate the quick triage.

lia: I'll follow up on the telemetry dashboards once kevin has initial metrics in the PR.
